source_text:
Στίχ. κζ΄. Ψυχὴ ἐὰν ἁμάρτῃ ἀκουσίως. φησὶ. καὶ μὴ ποιήσῃ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἐντολῶν Κυρίου, ὧν δεῖ ποιεῖν.
(12) Εἰ δὲ κατὰ φύσιν ἔχει. Ἔστι τάχα τινὰ προστάγματα Κυρίου, ἃ οὐ δεῖ ποιεῖν, κατὰ τό· Ἕδωξαν αὐτοῖς προστάγματα οὐ καλά. Ψυχὴ οὖν ἁμαρτάνει ἀκουσίως, ὅτε προφάσει εὐσεβείας τὸ μὴ δέον τηρεῖ. Καὶ δεῖται θυσίας πρὸς ἄφεσιν, οὐ δεομένου θυσίας τοῦ δρῶντος ἐξεπίτηδες· ὡς ὁ γεγονὼς Ἰουδαῖος, ἵνα Ἰουδαίους κερδήσῃ, καὶ περιτεμὼν τὸν Τιμόθεον.
Στίχ. κη΄. Σημαίνει οὖν, ὅτι ἀμσρτία καλεῖται καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ προσαγόμενον. Οὕτω νοητέον τό· Ἁμαρτίας λαοῦ μου φάγονται. Εἰ οὖν ὁ ἁμαρτάνων αὐτὴν δοκεῖ θύειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῷ μετανοεῖν, οὐκ ὀφείλει τοῖς αὐτοῖς περιπίπτειν, ἐπεὶ ἀναζῇ ἡ ἁμαρτία. Οὕτω δυνατὸν τὸν Χριστὸν καλεῖν ἀμαρείαν, ὡς ὑπὸρ τῆς πάντων ἁμαρτίας τυθέντα.
thought_title: Unintentional sin by keeping a command under pretext of piety
orientation: Origen is commenting on Leviticus 4:27, explaining what it means for a soul to sin unintentionally and why such a sin requires sacrifice.
pass_a_gloss: Verse 27. A soul, if it sins unintentionally, it says, and does not do any of all the commandments of the Lord, which it is necessary to do. (12) But if it has according to nature. There are perhaps certain ordinances of the Lord, which it is not necessary to do, according to the saying: They seemed to themselves ordinances not good. A soul therefore sins unintentionally, when under pretext of piety it keeps what is not necessary. And it needs sacrifice for forgiveness, while the one acting deliberately does not need sacrifice; as the one who became a Jew, in order that he might gain Jews, and circumcised Timothy. Verse 28. It signifies therefore, that the thing being offered is itself also called sin. Thus must be understood the saying: The sins of my people they will eat. If therefore the one sinning seems to sacrifice the sin itself in repenting, he ought not to fall into the same things, since the sin comes to life again. Thus it is possible to call Christ sin, as having been sacrificed for the sin of all.

choices.english: A soul, if it sins unintentionally
choices.why: Keeps the conditional force and the glossary rendering of ἀκουσίως as unintentionally
rejected: If a soul sins without intent

choices.english: which it is necessary to do
choices.why: Preserves the impersonal δεῖ as necessity, distinguishing these from commands that need not be done

choices.term: Ἔστι τάχα τινὰ προστάγματα Κυρίου, ἃ οὐ δεῖ ποιεῖν
choices.english: There are perhaps certain ordinances of the Lord, which it is not necessary to do
choices.why: Keeps τάχα as perhaps and the same δεῖ construction to show the contrast with the previous clause
rejected: There are maybe some commandments of the Lord which should not be done

choices.why: Renders προφάσει as pretext, capturing the deceptive or false justification Origen describes

choices.english: the sin comes to life again
choices.why: Keeps the vivid metaphor of sin reviving, which Origen uses to warn against falling back into sin

choices.english: as having been sacrificed for the sin of all
choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering of ἁμαρτία as sin and keeps the passive participle to show Christ as the one sacrificed
rejected: as being offered for the sin of all

bible_refs.note: Ψυχὴ ἐὰν ἁμάρτῃ ἀκουσίως... καὶ μὴ ποιήσῃ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἐντολῶν Κυρίου, ὧν δεῖ ποιεῖν

pass_b_english: Verse 27: “A soul, if it sins unintentionally,” it says, “and does not do any of all the commandments of the Lord, which it is necessary to do.”

But consider what is natural here. There are perhaps certain ordinances of the Lord which it is not necessary to do, according to the text: “They gave themselves ordinances that were not good” (Ezekiel 20:25). So a soul sins unintentionally when it keeps what it should not keep under pretext of piety. And this requires a sacrifice for forgiveness, whereas the one who acts deliberately does not require a sacrifice—like the one who became a Jew in order to gain Jews, and circumcised Timothy.

Verse 28: It indicates, then, that the very thing being offered is also called sin. This is how we must understand the text: “They will eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4:8). If, then, the one who sins seems to offer the sin itself as a sacrifice in repenting, he ought not to fall back into the same sins, since the sin comes to life again. In this way it is possible to call Christ sin, as having been sacrificed for the sin of all.
notes: The source has ἀμσρτία (with metathesis) in the clause Σημαίνει οὖν, ὅτι ἀμσρτία καλεῖται; this is likely a scribal error for ἁμαρτία, and the gloss renders it as sin.
The source has ἀμαρείαν in the final clause Οὕτω δυνατὸν τὸν Χριστὸν καλεῖν ἀμαρείαν; this is likely a scribal error for ἁμαρτίαν, and the gloss renders it as sin.
